title: TU-GET ชุดฝึกที่ 4

groups.instructionTh: เลือกคำหรือวลีที่เหมาะสมที่สุดเติมในช่องว่าง เพื่อให้ประโยคถูกต้องตามหลักไวยากรณ์

items.stem: Not until the final data set had been cross-checked ____ to publish the findings.
items.explanationTh: เมื่อขึ้นต้นด้วย "Not until ..." ประโยคหลักต้องสลับกริยาช่วยไว้หน้าประธาน (inversion) จึงเป็น "did the team agree" ส่วนตัวเลือกอื่นไม่สลับหรือสลับผิดรูป

items.stem: The admissions committee recommended that every applicant ____ a portfolio of recent work before the interview.
items.explanationTh: หลังกริยา recommend + that ใช้ subjunctive คือกริยารูปพื้นฐาน (base form) ไม่ว่าประธานจะเป็นอะไร จึงตอบ "submit"

items.stem: Had the engineers tested the bridge under winter conditions, the cracks ____ much earlier.
items.explanationTh: "Had the engineers tested ..." คือ If-clause แบบที่ 3 ที่ละ if แล้วสลับ had ไว้หน้า ประโยคหลักจึงต้องเป็น would have + V3 และรอยร้าว "ถูกตรวจพบ" จึงใช้ passive "would have been detected"

items.stem: ____ in a remote valley, the village was largely untouched by the tourism boom of the 1990s.
items.explanationTh: หมู่บ้าน "ถูกตั้งอยู่" ในหุบเขา ความหมายเป็น passive จึงใช้ past participle "Situated" ขึ้นต้นวลี ส่วน Situating/Having situated เป็นความหมายเชิงกระทำ

items.stem: The proposal, ____ was debated for nearly three hours, was eventually shelved.
items.explanationTh: อนุประโยคที่อยู่ระหว่างจุลภาคเป็น non-defining relative clause ซึ่งใช้ that ไม่ได้ และต้องการสรรพนามแทนสิ่งของที่เป็นประธาน จึงใช้ "which"

items.stem: So persuasive ____ that even the most sceptical members of the panel changed their votes.
items.explanationTh: โครงสร้าง "So + adjective" ขึ้นต้นประโยคต้องสลับกริยาไว้หน้าประธาน และกริยาหลักคือ be จึงเป็น "was her argument" ไม่ใช้ did กับ be

items.stem: It is high time the city council ____ something about the flooding in the eastern districts.
items.explanationTh: สำนวน "It is high time + ประธาน" ตามด้วยกริยาช่องที่ 2 (past simple) เพื่อบอกว่าควรทำได้แล้ว จึงตอบ "did"

items.stem: By the time the new regulations take effect next year, most firms ____ their reporting systems.
items.explanationTh: "By the time ... take effect next year" บอกจุดเวลาในอนาคต การกระทำที่จะเสร็จก่อนจุดนั้นใช้ future perfect "will have updated"

items.stem: Scarcely had the guest lecture begun ____ the fire alarm went off.
items.explanationTh: โครงสร้าง "Scarcely/Hardly had ... when ..." ใช้คู่กับ when ส่วน than ใช้คู่กับ No sooner

items.stem: The more carefully a hypothesis is framed, ____ to test it becomes.
items.explanationTh: โครงสร้างเปรียบเทียบคู่ขนาน "The more ..., the + comparative ..." จึงต้องเป็น "the easier"

items.stem: Neither the director nor the board members ____ aware of the accounting error until the audit.
items.explanationTh: กับ neither ... nor ... กริยาผันตามประธานตัวที่อยู่ใกล้กว่า คือ "the board members" ซึ่งเป็นพหูพจน์ และเหตุการณ์เป็นอดีต จึงใช้ "were"

items.stem: The manuscript is thought ____ in a monastery library before being sold in the eighteenth century.
items.explanationTh: การกระทำ (ถูกเก็บรักษา) เกิดก่อนเวลาที่ "is thought" และต้นฉบับเป็นผู้ถูกกระทำ จึงใช้ perfect passive infinitive "to have been kept"

items.stem: She would rather her students ____ their own research questions than copy them from a textbook.
items.explanationTh: "would rather + ประธานอื่น" ตามด้วยกริยาช่องที่ 2 เมื่อพูดถึงความต้องการในปัจจุบัน/อนาคต จึงตอบ "developed" ส่วน had developed ใช้กับเรื่องในอดีต

groups.instructionTh: แต่ละประโยคมีส่วนที่ขีดเส้นใต้ 4 ส่วน (A–D) เลือกส่วนที่ผิดหลักไวยากรณ์ ซึ่งมีเพียงส่วนเดียว

items.stem: The number of students [[who enroll]] in online courses [[have risen]] steadily [[over the past]] decade, [[according to]] the survey.
items.explanationTh: "The number of ..." เป็นประธานเอกพจน์ กริยาต้องเป็น "has risen" ไม่ใช่ have risen (ต่างจาก "A number of ..." ที่ใช้พหูพจน์)

items.stem: [[Despite of]] the heavy rain, the organizers [[decided]] to hold the ceremony [[outdoors]] [[as planned]].
items.explanationTh: despite ไม่ใช้คู่กับ of ต้องเป็น "Despite the heavy rain" หรือ "In spite of the heavy rain"

items.stem: The researchers [[could not]] [[explain]] to the panel [[exactly]] [[why did the samples]] change colour so rapidly.
items.explanationTh: คำถามที่ซ้อนอยู่ในประโยค (embedded question) ต้องเรียงแบบประโยคบอกเล่า คือ "why the samples changed" ไม่ใช้ did

items.stem: The professor [[suggested]] that the class [[spend]] more time [[to discuss]] the primary sources [[before]] the exam.
items.explanationTh: สำนวน "spend time + V-ing" จึงต้องเป็น "discussing" ส่วน "spend" หลัง suggested that ถูกต้องตามหลัก subjunctive

items.stem: The new library, [[which]] opened last month, [[has attracted]] more visitors [[than]] [[expecting]].
items.explanationTh: ต้องเป็น "than expected" (ที่ถูกคาดไว้) ใช้ past participle เพราะผู้เยี่ยมชม "ถูกคาดการณ์" ไม่ใช่ expecting

items.stem: Not only [[the museum lacks]] funding, but it [[also]] struggles [[to attract]] [[younger]] visitors.
items.explanationTh: เมื่อขึ้นต้นด้วย "Not only" ต้องสลับกริยาช่วยไว้หน้าประธาน คือ "does the museum lack"

items.stem: The committee [[is looking forward]] to [[receive]] your application [[and]] will contact you [[shortly]].
items.explanationTh: "look forward to" ใช้ to เป็นบุพบท ต้องตามด้วยคำนามหรือ V-ing คือ "receiving"

items.stem: It was [[such a]] complicated experiment [[that]] [[few of]] the assistants [[could understood]] the procedure.
items.explanationTh: หลัง modal verb (could) ต้องใช้กริยารูปพื้นฐาน คือ "could understand"

items.stem: The harbour town, [[known]] for [[its]] seafood market, [[have]] become [[increasingly]] popular with cyclists.
items.explanationTh: ประธานคือ "The harbour town" เป็นเอกพจน์ กริยาต้องเป็น "has become" วลีระหว่างจุลภาคไม่มีผลต่อการผันกริยา

items.stem: The volunteers [[were told]] not to touch the fossils, [[most of them]] were [[extremely]] [[fragile]].
items.explanationTh: การเชื่อมสองประโยคด้วยจุลภาคต้องใช้ relative pronoun คือ "most of which" (ซึ่งส่วนใหญ่) การใช้ them ทำให้เป็นสองประโยคเชื่อมกันผิด (comma splice)

items.stem: She [[has been working]] at the observatory [[since]] 2019, so she [[is knowing]] its instruments better than [[anyone else]].
items.explanationTh: know เป็น stative verb ไม่ใช้ในรูป continuous ต้องเป็น "she knows" ส่วน "has been working ... since 2019" ถูกต้องตามหลัก present perfect continuous

items.stem: [[The]] information [[that]] the farmers provided [[were]] [[surprisingly]] detailed.
items.explanationTh: information เป็นคำนามนับไม่ได้ ใช้กริยาเอกพจน์ "was" ไม่ใช่ were

groups.instructionTh: เลือกคำที่เหมาะสมที่สุดเติมในช่องว่าง หรือเลือกคำ/วลีที่มีความหมายใกล้เคียงที่สุดกับคำที่กำหนด

items.stem: The results were so ____ that the journal requested a second, independent analysis before publication.
items.explanationTh: anomalous = ผิดปกติ ผิดไปจากที่คาด จึงทำให้วารสารต้องขอให้วิเคราะห์ซ้ำ ส่วน mundane (ธรรมดา) และ coherent (สอดคล้องกัน) ไม่ใช่เหตุให้ต้องตรวจซ้ำ

items.stem: In the sentence "New drainage channels helped mitigate the effects of the flood," the word "mitigate" is closest in meaning to
items.explanationTh: mitigate = ทำให้เบาบางลง ลดความรุนแรง ใกล้เคียงกับ lessen

items.stem: Her account of the mountain expedition was so ____ that readers felt they were travelling alongside her.
items.explanationTh: vivid = มีชีวิตชีวา เห็นภาพชัด จึงทำให้ผู้อ่านรู้สึกเหมือนร่วมเดินทาง ส่วน vicarious ใช้กับประสบการณ์ของผู้อ่าน (vicarious experience) ไม่ใช้บรรยายตัวงานเขียน และ verbatim แปลว่าคำต่อคำ

items.stem: "Auditors will scrutinize every invoice submitted last year." The word "scrutinize" is closest in meaning to
items.explanationTh: scrutinize = ตรวจสอบอย่างละเอียดถี่ถ้วนทุกรายการ ตรงกับ examine closely ส่วน check randomly คือสุ่มตรวจ ขัดกับคำว่า every invoice

items.stem: Because the instructions were ____, half of the participants completed the task incorrectly.
items.explanationTh: ambiguous = กำกวม ตีความได้หลายทาง จึงเป็นเหตุให้คนทำผิดครึ่งหนึ่ง ส่วน meticulous, thorough, explicit ล้วนมีความหมายเชิงบวกว่าละเอียด/ชัดเจน

items.stem: "Rising shipping costs have steadily eroded the company's profits." The word "eroded" is closest in meaning to
items.explanationTh: erode = กัดกร่อน ค่อย ๆ ลดลง คำว่า steadily ช่วยยืนยันว่าเป็นการลดลงทีละน้อย

items.stem: The professor is admired for her ____ approach to research: she checks every source and questions every assumption, including her own.
items.explanationTh: rigorous = เข้มงวด รอบคอบ สอดคล้องกับการตรวจทุกแหล่งข้อมูลและตั้งคำถามกับทุกสมมติฐาน ส่วน haphazard (สะเปะสะปะ) และ gullible (เชื่อคนง่าย) ตรงข้าม

items.stem: "The new survey corroborates the guide's account of where the old harbour wall stood." The word "corroborates" is closest in meaning to
items.explanationTh: corroborate = ยืนยัน สนับสนุนว่าเป็นความจริง ตรงกับ confirms

items.stem: The annual craft fair has become ____ part of the town's identity; residents cannot imagine the year without it.
items.explanationTh: integral = เป็นส่วนสำคัญที่ขาดไม่ได้ สอดคล้องกับ "cannot imagine the year without it" ส่วน peripheral (ชายขอบ) และ superficial (ผิวเผิน) ขัดกับบริบท

items.stem: "Funding for the second phase is contingent on the results of the pilot study." The phrase "contingent on" is closest in meaning to
items.explanationTh: contingent on = ขึ้นอยู่กับ คือทุนระยะที่สองจะได้หรือไม่ขึ้นอยู่กับผลการศึกษานำร่อง

items.stem: The two theories are not ____; a researcher can reasonably accept both at the same time.
items.explanationTh: incompatible = ขัดแย้งกัน ไปด้วยกันไม่ได้ เมื่อทฤษฎี "ไม่ขัดแย้งกัน" จึงยอมรับทั้งสองได้พร้อมกัน

items.stem: "The museum's collection was greatly augmented by a private donation." The word "augmented" is closest in meaning to
items.explanationTh: augment = เพิ่มขึ้น ขยายให้มากขึ้น การบริจาคทำให้คอลเลกชันใหญ่ขึ้น จึงตรงกับ enlarged ส่วน appraised (ประเมินราคา) และ restored (บูรณะ) ไม่ได้หมายถึงการเพิ่มจำนวน

items.stem: Critics argued that the consultants' report ____ the risks of the plan while exaggerating its benefits.
items.explanationTh: understate = กล่าวน้อยกว่าความจริง ซึ่งตรงข้ามกับ exaggerating ในประโยคเดียวกัน ส่วน underlined (เน้นย้ำ) ไม่เข้ากับการเปรียบเทียบนี้

items.stem: "Her explanation was plausible, though not entirely convincing." The word "plausible" is closest in meaning to
items.explanationTh: plausible = ฟังดูมีเหตุผล น่าเชื่อได้ ตรงกับ reasonable ส่วน persuasive และ proven ขัดกับ "though not entirely convincing"

items.stem: After months of negotiation, the two firms finally reached a ____ that both sides could accept.
items.explanationTh: reach a compromise = ได้ข้อตกลงที่ต่างฝ่ายต่างยอมกันคนละครึ่ง เข้ากับ "both sides could accept"

items.stem: "The scientist was reluctant to extrapolate from such a small sample." The word "extrapolate" is closest in meaning to
items.explanationTh: extrapolate = อนุมานหรือขยายผลจากข้อมูลที่มีไปสู่ข้อสรุปที่กว้างขึ้น นักวิทยาศาสตร์ลังเลเพราะกลุ่มตัวอย่างเล็กเกินไป

items.stem: The village's population has ____ from 3,000 to fewer than 800 as young people move to the cities.
items.explanationTh: dwindle = ค่อย ๆ ลดน้อยลง ตรงกับตัวเลขที่ลดจาก 3,000 เหลือไม่ถึง 800 ส่วน stagnated (หยุดนิ่ง) และ fluctuated (ขึ้น ๆ ลง ๆ) ไม่ตรงกับการลดลงต่อเนื่อง

items.stem: "The new timetable had several unforeseen ramifications for students who commute." The word "ramifications" is closest in meaning to
items.explanationTh: ramifications = ผลที่ตามมา (มักไม่ได้คาดไว้) ตรงกับ consequences

items.stem: The tour guide gave a ____ summary of the castle's history, covering six centuries in under five minutes.
items.explanationTh: succinct = กระชับ ได้ใจความ สอดคล้องกับการเล่าประวัติหกศตวรรษในเวลาไม่ถึงห้านาที ส่วน successive (ต่อเนื่องกัน) และ sustained (ยืดเยื้อ) หน้าตาคล้ายแต่ความหมายไม่เข้ากับบริบท

items.stem: "The new manager proved adept at resolving disagreements among staff." The word "adept" is closest in meaning to
items.explanationTh: adept at = ชำนาญ เก่งในเรื่องใดเรื่องหนึ่ง ตรงกับ skilled ส่วน adaptable (ปรับตัวได้) หน้าตาคล้าย adept แต่ความหมายต่างกัน

items.stem: Many early inventors worked in ____, unaware that others elsewhere were trying to solve the same problem.
items.explanationTh: work in isolation = ทำงานโดดเดี่ยว ไม่ติดต่อกับผู้อื่น สอดคล้องกับ "unaware that others ..." ส่วน insulation (ฉนวน) เป็นคำหน้าตาคล้าย และ collaboration ขัดกับบริบท

items.stem: "The evidence for the theory remains tenuous." The word "tenuous" is closest in meaning to
items.explanationTh: tenuous = บอบบาง อ่อน ไม่มีน้ำหนัก ตรงกับ weak ส่วน tenacious (เหนียวแน่น) หน้าตาคล้ายแต่ความหมายต่างกัน และ conclusive มีความหมายตรงข้าม

items.stem: The bridge was closed as a ____ measure while engineers inspected the cracks.
items.explanationTh: precautionary measure = มาตรการป้องกันไว้ก่อน ปิดสะพานระหว่างตรวจรอยร้าวเพื่อความปลอดภัย ส่วน punitive แปลว่าเพื่อลงโทษ

items.stem: "Several reviewers dismissed the band's second album as derivative." The word "derivative" is closest in meaning to
items.explanationTh: derivative ในบริบทงานศิลปะ = ลอกเลียนหรือดัดแปลงจากงานอื่น ไม่มีความเป็นต้นฉบับ คำว่า dismissed บอกว่าเป็นคำวิจารณ์เชิงลบ

items.stem: Despite the ____ of information available online, finding reliable sources can still be surprisingly difficult.
items.explanationTh: abundance = ความมีอยู่มากมาย คำว่า Despite แสดงความขัดแย้ง: ข้อมูลมีมาก แต่หาแหล่งที่เชื่อถือได้ยาก

groups.instructionTh: อ่านบทความ แล้วตอบคำถามโดยเลือกคำตอบที่ถูกต้องที่สุด
groups.title: Measuring the World with Fragile Atoms
groups.text:
For most of the twentieth century, the word "quantum" conjured up images of particle accelerators and thought experiments rather than practical tools. That perception is changing. A new generation of quantum sensors, devices that exploit the extreme sensitivity of atoms to their surroundings, is moving out of physics laboratories and into fields as varied as archaeology, civil engineering and navigation.

The principle behind these instruments is, in one sense, a turning of weakness into strength. Quantum states are notoriously fragile: a stray magnetic field, a slight change in temperature or a passing vibration can disturb them. For engineers trying to build quantum computers, this fragility is the central obstacle, since any disturbance corrupts the information being processed. Sensor designers, however, regard the same property as an asset. If a cloud of atoms reacts measurably to a change in gravity a billion times smaller than the pull we feel every day, then that cloud can be used to detect the change.

Consider the quantum gravimeter. In a typical design, atoms are cooled with lasers to a fraction of a degree above absolute zero and then allowed to fall inside a vacuum chamber. As they fall, further laser pulses split each atom's wave into two paths that later recombine. The pattern produced when the paths meet depends on how strongly gravity acted on the atoms during their fall. Because local gravity varies slightly with the density of the ground below, a sufficiently precise gravimeter can reveal hidden structures: an empty tunnel, a buried wall, a pocket of groundwater.

A team at the fictional Halvorsen Institute of Applied Physics demonstrated this last year by surveying a field where old estate records suggested a medieval cellar had once stood. Conventional ground-penetrating radar had produced unclear results because of the clay-rich soil. The quantum device, by contrast, identified a void roughly two metres below the surface, and a small excavation later confirmed the cellar's outline. "We didn't need to dig twenty test pits," noted Ingrid Solberg, the project's lead engineer. "We dug one."

Navigation offers a second promising application. Satellite positioning is convenient, but its signals are weak and can be blocked underwater, underground or by interference. Quantum accelerometers, which track motion by measuring how atoms respond to acceleration, could allow ships and trains to calculate their position for long periods without any external signal. Prototype models drift by only a few hundred metres over a day-long voyage, compared with several kilometres for the best conventional inertial systems.

Yet enthusiasm should be tempered by practical realities. Most quantum sensors still require bulky lasers, vacuum pumps and careful shielding, which makes them expensive and difficult to operate outside controlled environments. The Halvorsen gravimeter, for instance, weighs over 150 kilograms and needed a team of four to transport and calibrate. Moreover, measurements take time: to average out background noise, the device sometimes has to remain in one spot for twenty minutes. For a survey covering several square kilometres, this is a serious limitation.

Researchers are therefore concentrating less on improving sensitivity, which is already remarkable, and more on miniaturisation and robustness. Several groups are developing chip-scale components that could shrink the laser systems to the size of a shoebox. If they succeed, the next decade may see quantum sensors become as routine on construction sites as surveying tripods are today, though few in the field expect that transition to be quick.

items.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
options: The coming replacement of satellite navigation systems
Why quantum computers remain impractical for engineers
A medieval cellar discovered with a new technology
Sensors that exploit quantum fragility, and their limits
items.explanationTh: บทความพูดถึงเซนเซอร์ควอนตัมที่ใช้ความเปราะบางของสถานะควอนตัมมาวัดค่า ทั้งการประยุกต์ใช้และข้อจำกัด (ย่อหน้า 6–7) ส่วนห้องใต้ดินยุคกลางเป็นเพียงตัวอย่างหนึ่ง

items.stem: What does the author mean by "a turning of weakness into strength" in paragraph 2?
options: Sensor designers have solved the main problem facing computing
Fragile atoms can be made stronger by cooling them with lasers
A property that hinders quantum computing makes sensing possible
Weak gravitational fields are easier to measure than strong ones

groups.instructionTh: อ่านบทความ แล้วตอบคำถามโดยเลือกคำตอบที่ถูกต้องที่สุด
groups.title: The Slow Reach of Interest Rates
groups.text:
When a central bank raises its main interest rate, the effects do not arrive all at once. Economists have long described monetary policy as operating with "long and variable lags": a rate decision taken today may not reach its full impact on prices for eighteen months or more. This delay creates a peculiar problem for policymakers. They must act on forecasts of an economy they cannot yet see, knowing that by the time their decisions take effect, conditions may have shifted entirely.

The transmission of a rate change works through several channels. The most direct is the cost of borrowing. Higher rates make mortgages, business loans and credit card balances more expensive, discouraging spending and investment. A second channel runs through asset prices: when savings accounts and government bonds offer better returns, investors are less willing to pay high prices for shares and property, and households that feel less wealthy tend to cut back. A third channel is the exchange rate. Higher domestic rates attract foreign capital, strengthening the currency and making imported goods cheaper, which directly lowers measured inflation.

Each channel, however, depends on circumstances. In Varenland, a fictional economy often used in textbook exercises, most homeowners hold mortgages whose rates are fixed for ten years. A rate rise there barely affects household budgets until those mortgages come up for renewal, so the borrowing channel is weak and slow. In neighbouring Ostmark, where nearly all mortgages carry variable rates, the same rise shows up in monthly repayments within weeks. Identical decisions can thus produce strikingly different outcomes depending on the structure of a country's financial system.

Because of these complications, central banks increasingly rely on a fourth tool that costs almost nothing to deploy: communication. The idea, known as forward guidance, is that by signalling the likely path of future rates, a central bank can influence long-term borrowing costs and expectations immediately, without waiting for actual rate changes to work through the economy. If businesses believe that inflation will return to target, they are less likely to raise prices pre-emptively, and workers are less likely to demand wage increases that would push costs up further. Expectations, in other words, can become self-fulfilling.

Forward guidance is not without risks. Its power rests entirely on credibility, and credibility is easier to lose than to build. If a central bank promises to keep rates low "for an extended period" and then reverses course a few months later, markets may discount its future statements. Some economists also worry that overly precise guidance ties policymakers' hands: having committed publicly to a particular path, a bank may hesitate to change direction even when new data clearly call for it, simply to avoid appearing inconsistent.

There is, finally, the question of audience. Statements crafted for bond traders, who parse every adjective, may mean little to the shopkeepers and families whose expectations matter most for inflation. A survey by the fictional Lindqvist Economic Forum found that fewer than one in five Varenland adults could correctly state whether the central bank's last move had been an increase or a cut. Several central banks have responded by publishing plain-language summaries alongside their technical reports, using short sentences and everyday examples. The aim is a welcome one. Whether such efforts genuinely reshape public expectations, or merely reassure the institutions producing them, remains an open question.

groups.instructionTh: อ่านบทความ แล้วตอบคำถามโดยเลือกคำตอบที่ถูกต้องที่สุด
groups.title: Patterns Across Languages
groups.text:
Linguists who compare the world's languages quickly discover that there are far fewer basic patterns than one might expect. Of the six logically possible orders of subject (S), verb (V) and object (O) in a simple sentence, two account for the great majority of languages. Subject-object-verb, as in Japanese or Turkish, and subject-verb-object, as in English or Thai, together cover roughly three-quarters of the languages for which reliable descriptions exist. Orders in which the object comes before the subject are so rare that, for decades, some scholars doubted they existed at all.

The study of such patterns is called linguistic typology. Its practitioners are less interested in the history of any particular language than in the range of variation across all of them, and in the constraints that seem to limit it. One of the field's most influential discoveries is that certain features tend to cluster. Languages in which the verb comes last usually place their equivalent of prepositions after the noun as well, so that they have "postpositions" rather than prepositions, and they tend to put possessors before the thing possessed. Verb-initial languages show the opposite tendencies. These correlations, sometimes called implicational universals, take the form "if a language has feature X, it will probably have feature Y."

Why should such regularities exist? One family of explanations appeals to processing efficiency. A language that consistently places "heads", the words that determine a phrase's grammatical character, on the same side of their dependents may be easier for listeners to process in real time, because they can apply a single strategy throughout. Laboratory experiments in which volunteers learn small artificial languages lend some support to this view: participants exposed to inconsistent word orders tend, without being told to, to regularise them into more harmonious patterns.

A second family of explanations is historical. Languages that share an ancestor naturally inherit many features, and languages spoken in the same region borrow from one another, even when they are unrelated. If one were to count every language in a large, closely related family as an independent data point, apparent universals might simply reflect the success of a few ancestral languages that happened to have particular traits. Careful typologists therefore build samples that include only one or two languages from each family and each geographical area, though critics note that the choice of which languages to include can itself shape the results.

The tension between these explanations came to a head in a study by the fictional Corvallis Linguistic Database team, who traced word-order changes along the reconstructed family trees of several large language groups. If processing pressures were universal, they argued, features should change together in the same way in every family. Instead, they found that linked changes were common in some families but almost absent in others. Their conclusion was not that cognitive explanations are wrong, but that they operate alongside lineage-specific factors that no single principle can predict.

For students of English, typology offers a useful corrective to the assumption that one's own language represents a natural default. English's subject-verb-object order, its prepositions and its reliance on word order rather than word endings to show who did what to whom are not inevitable features of human language. They are one solution among many, and speakers of Turkish or Japanese manage perfectly well with quite different ones.

groups.instructionTh: อ่านบทความ แล้วตอบคำถามโดยเลือกคำตอบที่ถูกต้องที่สุด
groups.title: Who Pays for an Invasion?
groups.text:
When an invasive plant or animal establishes itself in a new environment, ecologists tend to describe the damage in terms of lost biodiversity. Economists, increasingly, are asking a different question: who pays, and how much? The answer matters because decisions about whether and how to fight an invasion are ultimately decisions about how to spend limited public money.

The costs fall into two broad categories. Direct damages include crops eaten, water pipes clogged and timber destroyed. In the fictional river province of Maralinga Basin, an invasive freshwater mussel that arrived in the ballast water of cargo ships attached itself to the intake pipes of a hydroelectric plant, forcing operators to shut down turbines for cleaning several times a year. Each shutdown cost the plant roughly 400,000 dollars in lost generation. Management costs, the second category, cover everything spent on prevention, monitoring and removal: inspection stations for boats, trained detection dogs, chemical treatments and the labour of volunteers who pull weeds from riverbanks.

A striking pattern emerges when these costs are tracked over time. Spending on prevention is typically tiny compared with spending on control once an invader is established. A widely cited model developed by the fictional Okonjo Centre for Environmental Economics suggests that a dollar invested in early detection can avoid between ten and a hundred dollars of later costs. The logic is intuitive: a population of a few hundred individuals can often be eradicated relatively cheaply, whereas one of several million may only ever be contained.

Why, then, do governments so often under-invest in prevention? Part of the answer lies in the nature of the benefits. The success of a prevention programme is invisible: nothing happens. It is difficult to win support, or budgets, for averting a disaster that the public never sees. Damages from an established invader, by contrast, are concrete and attract attention, so resources tend to flow towards visible crises rather than quiet risks.

A further complication is that costs and benefits are rarely borne by the same people. The shipping companies whose vessels carry stowaway organisms seldom pay for the invasions they cause; those costs fall on farmers, utilities and taxpayers, often in places far from any port. Economists describe this as an externality, a cost imposed on third parties that is not reflected in the price of the activity that generates it. Some have proposed charging a small fee on imports from high-risk regions to fund inspection programmes, in effect making the polluter pay. Opponents argue that such fees are difficult to calibrate and could become trade barriers in disguise.

Not every introduced species is purely a liability. Some provide services that partly offset their damage: an introduced shrub may stabilise eroding slopes, or a non-native fish may support a commercial fishery. Assigning monetary values to these benefits is contentious, and critics warn that doing so may give a misleading impression of balance where ecological harm is severe and irreversible. Nonetheless, most economists in the field agree that ignoring benefits altogether produces worse decisions than attempting to measure them, however imperfectly.

groups.instructionTh: อ่านบทความ แล้วตอบคำถามโดยเลือกคำตอบที่ถูกต้องที่สุด
groups.title: The Business Behind the Brush
groups.text:
Visitors to the great galleries of Europe often admire Renaissance paintings as the products of individual genius. The reality behind many of these works was considerably more commercial. Most painters in fifteenth-century Italy did not create art and then look for buyers; they worked to order, under detailed contracts drawn up by the patrons who paid them. Understanding these arrangements does not diminish the achievements of the artists, but it does change how we read the works themselves.

Surviving contracts reveal how much patrons sought to control. A typical agreement specified the subject of the painting, the number of figures, the size of the panel and the deadline for completion. Many also regulated materials, and here money spoke loudly. Ultramarine, a deep blue pigment ground from a semi-precious stone imported from Central Asia, cost more than gold by weight. Contracts often stipulated that the robe of the central figure be painted in ultramarine "of the finest quality, at two florins the ounce", ensuring that the patron's devotion, and wealth, would be visible to everyone who saw the work.

Over the course of the century, however, a subtle shift took place. Earlier contracts devoted most of their attention to materials, measuring the value of a painting largely by the cost of what went into it. Later agreements increasingly emphasised the artist's own labour. A contract drafted in 1487 for the fictional painter Matteo Varri, for example, required that "all the figures be painted by Matteo's own hand, and especially the faces", rather than by his assistants. The patron was now paying not only for precious blue but for the master's skill, a sign that artistic talent itself was becoming a form of conspicuous expenditure.

Patrons had varied motives. Wealthy merchant families commissioned altarpieces partly as expressions of faith, but also to display their status in a society where commerce was sometimes viewed with suspicion. Guilds funded public sculptures to advertise their prosperity and to compete with rival guilds. City authorities ordered large wall paintings for council halls to project an image of good government. In each case, the work served purposes that went well beyond decoration.

Artists were not merely passive executors of these wishes. The most successful negotiated terms, raised their prices as their reputations grew, and occasionally exploited vague contract language to introduce their own ideas. Varri's letters, preserved in a family archive, show him gently persuading a patron to replace a crowded scene of twelve figures with a quieter composition of four, arguing that "a few figures well made bring more honour than many made in haste". The patron agreed, and the finished panel is now considered one of Varri's finest works.

Recognising the role of patrons helps explain features of Renaissance art that might otherwise seem puzzling: the small kneeling figures of donors tucked into the corners of scenes, the coats of arms painted on frames, the striking prominence of blue. These are not distractions from the art but evidence of the economic and social world that made it possible. To look at a Renaissance altarpiece in this light is to read a kind of document, one that records not only an artistic vision but also a negotiation between those who paid and those who painted.

groups.instructionTh: อ่านบทความ แล้วตอบคำถามโดยเลือกคำตอบที่ถูกต้องที่สุด
groups.title: When Software Inherits Prejudice
groups.text:
Automated decision systems are often promoted as a cure for human prejudice. A loan officer may be swayed by an applicant's accent; a hiring manager may favour candidates who attended the same university as she did. Software, the argument goes, applies the same rules to everyone. Yet a growing body of research shows that algorithms can reproduce, and sometimes amplify, the very biases they were meant to remove.

The problem usually begins with data. Machine-learning systems learn patterns from historical examples, and history is not neutral. Suppose a company trains a program to identify promising job applicants using records of whom it hired and promoted over the past twenty years. If, during that period, the company rarely promoted people from a particular background, the program may learn to rate such applicants poorly, not because anyone instructed it to, but because it has faithfully absorbed the patterns in its training data. The algorithm, in effect, mistakes past discrimination for evidence of merit.

Removing sensitive categories from the data does not necessarily solve the problem. Even if a system is never told an applicant's gender or ethnicity, other variables can serve as proxies. Home address may correlate with ethnicity; gaps in employment may correlate with caring responsibilities that fall disproportionately on women; the clubs or hobbies listed on a CV may hint at social class. A model hungry for any signal that predicts its target will exploit these correlations unless it is specifically designed not to.

Measurement creates further difficulties. Developers must choose what their system is trying to predict, and the most convenient target is not always the most appropriate. In one widely discussed case study, a fictional city's road-maintenance tool was meant to identify streets most in need of repair. Because the actual condition of every street was costly to survey, the tool used the number of resident complaints as a substitute. Neighbourhoods where residents had less free time or less access to the city's online reporting system complained less often, and their roads were judged to need less attention, even when they were in worse condition.

Defining fairness is itself contested. A system might be considered fair if it approves the same proportion of applicants from each group, or if its error rates are equal across groups, or if applicants with the same score have the same actual chance of success regardless of group. Researchers at the fictional Brandt Institute for Computational Ethics have shown mathematically that, except in unusual circumstances, these definitions cannot all be satisfied at once. Choosing among them is therefore not a purely technical matter but a question of values, and not one that engineers should be left to settle alone.

None of this means that automated systems are necessarily worse than human judgement. Unlike a human decision-maker, an algorithm can be audited: its outputs can be tested systematically, its errors counted, and its rules adjusted. Several organisations now commission independent audits before introducing high-stakes systems, and some publish summaries of the results. Supporters argue that such transparency, if it became standard, could make automated decisions more accountable than the informal judgements they replace. The challenge is to ensure that audits are rigorous rather than ceremonial, and that their findings actually lead to change.
